added_claim_errors: "The 10%-per-year lifetime penalty" is imprecise: the penalty is 10% per full 12 months without Part B.
Presents 20+ employees as what "lets you delay Part B with no penalty". The SEP does not depend on employer size; the 20-employee line only decides who pays first.
"The drug coverage isn't creditable. Then you might need a Part D plan, and possibly Part B to get it." Misleading: Part D needs Part A or B enrollment, but the answer implies Part B specifically.
"Whether the plan requires you to enroll in Medicare at 65 (some do; most don't)": the frequency claim is unverifiable.
Says to call SSA at 1-800-772-1213 to withdraw an application before it takes effect: the withdrawal procedure is not verified. The phone number is the real SSA line.
The Federal Register link (FR-2025-11-19, 2025-20251) and the Medicare.gov links were not opened. The $202.90 figure matches the key.
Premium given as "roughly $185-$210/month, set annually": vague, and $185 is the 2025 figure. The 2026 standard premium is $202.90.
Frames the exception as active coverage "from an employer with 20+ employees", which implies employer size is a condition of the no-penalty SEP. It only decides who pays first.
"Coverage generally starts the month after Social Security processes your form": loosely worded and not verified.
"A few plans do [require Medicare] for certain employee classes": unverifiable.
Says SHIP counselors "deal with exactly this scenario constantly": unverifiable filler.
Says to sign up for Part D "at the same time" as Part B, without the 2-full-month window.
Says re-enrolling after CMS-1763 disenrollment is "more complicated" without detail. The form number CMS-1763 is real.
The Medicare.gov and shiphelp.org links were not opened, and the "HSA note" link points to the same working-past-65 page.

reasons: Both answers open by correcting the premise: don't enroll in Part B this month, the 8-month SEP applies, and the employer plan pays first. Both give the HSA and 6-month Part A backdating warning, explain how to decline Part B if already on Social Security, and keep CMS-L564 and the creditable-coverage notice. Both miss the IEP-end exception, and neither mentions CMS-40B or the online application. A gives the exact 2026 premium ($202.90, about $2,435 a year) and the 2-month Part D window, and is tighter. B is more complete: it asks HR to rule out COBRA and retiree coverage, asks about an HSA, states the 63-day Part D rule, and covers the Medigap window. But B gives a vague and partly outdated premium range ($185-$210), and it is longer, with padding such as the SHIP referral and the disenroll section. A has a small error about needing Part B for Part D and a loose "10%-per-year". The strengths and flaws roughly offset, so this is a tie.
